title: Stuffed Acorn Squash with Wheat Berries, Lentils & Walnuts
dek: Caramelized acorn squash halves hold a savory, chewy filling of wheat berries, lentils, browned mushrooms, red pepper and toasted walnuts for a satisfying plant-based centerpiece.
image_alt: Roasted acorn squash filled with wheat berries, lentils, mushrooms, red pepper, walnuts and fresh parsley
ingredients: 2 medium acorn squash, 1 1/2 to 1 3/4 lb each, scrubbed and dried
2/3 cup dry wheat berries, rinsed and drained
3 cups water, plus more if needed
1 1/4 tsp fine sea salt, divided, plus more to taste
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper, divided
1/3 cup walnut halves or pieces, coarsely chopped
1/2 medium red bell pepper, diced (about 1/2 cup)
3/4 cup canned brown or green lentils, rinsed and thoroughly drained
1/3 cup chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley, divided

instructions.name: Start the wheat berries
instructions.text: Put the rinsed wheat berries, 3 cups water and 1/4 teaspoon salt in a 3-quart saucepan. Bring to a boil, reduce to a steady simmer and partially cover. Cook 45 to 55 minutes, stirring twice and adding a splash of water if the pan looks dry, until the grains are plump and pleasantly chewy rather than hard. Drain very well; you should have about 1 1/2 cups cooked wheat berries.

instructions.name: Heat the oven and halve the squash
instructions.text: While the wheat berries cook, heat the oven to 425°F with a rack in the middle. Stabilize each squash on a nonslip towel, cut it from stem to tip with a sharp chef's knife, then scoop out the seeds and strings. Do not try to cut through a hard stem; finish the cut beside it and pull the halves apart.

instructions.name: Season and roast cut-side down
instructions.text: Mix 1 tablespoon olive oil with the maple syrup, 1/2 teaspoon salt and 1/4 teaspoon pepper. Brush it over the cut flesh and cavities. Arrange the four halves cut-side down on a heavy rimmed sheet pan and roast 35 to 45 minutes, until the flesh yields easily to a paring knife but the shells still hold their shape.

instructions.name: Toast the walnuts
instructions.text: While the squash roasts, heat a wide dry skillet over medium-low. Add the walnuts and cook 2 to 3 minutes, stirring often, until fragrant and a shade darker. Transfer them immediately to a plate so they do not scorch.

instructions.name: Brown the mushrooms and vegetables
instructions.text: Return the skillet to medium-high and add 1 tablespoon olive oil and the mushrooms. Cook 5 to 7 minutes, stirring only occasionally, until their released liquid evaporates and the edges brown. Add the onion, red pepper and remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt; cook 5 minutes until the onion softens. Stir in the garlic, thyme and smoked paprika for 30 seconds.

instructions.name: Build a cohesive savory filling
instructions.text: Reduce the heat to medium. Add 1 1/2 cups drained cooked wheat berries, the lentils, toasted walnuts, vinegar, remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil and remaining 1/4 teaspoon pepper. Cook 2 to 3 minutes, folding gently, until hot and no liquid pools in the skillet. Remove from the heat, fold in 1/4 cup parsley, then taste and adjust the salt.

instructions.name: Fill and finish the squash
instructions.text: Turn the roasted squash halves cut-side up. Divide the hot filling among the cavities, mounding it without packing. Return the pan to the 425°F oven for 8 to 10 minutes, until the tops are lightly crisp and the center of each portion reaches at least 165°F. Sprinkle with the remaining parsley and serve one half per person.

why_it_works: Roasting the squash cut-side down traps steam against the flesh while the oiled maple coating caramelizes where it touches the hot pan.
Wheat berries supply chewy structure, lentils make the filling substantial and chopped mushrooms add savory depth without disguising the individual ingredients visible in the finished dish.
Browning the mushrooms before adding onion prevents their released water from steaming every vegetable and leaving a loose filling.
Toasted walnuts echo the wheat berries' bite and add richness, while cider vinegar keeps the sweet squash and maple from tasting flat.
Draining both grains and lentils thoroughly lets the stuffing mound cleanly and protects the roasted squash from becoming watery during the final bake.
swaps: Replace wheat berries with 1 1/2 cups cooked farro for a similar chewy texture and a shorter stovetop cook. Neither grain is gluten-free.
For a gluten-free version, use 1 1/2 cups cooked brown rice or quinoa and verify that the lentils and spices were processed without gluten cross-contact.
Use canned chickpeas in place of lentils, chopping about one third of them so the filling stays cohesive instead of rolling out of the squash.
Pecans can replace walnuts measure for measure. For a nut-free dinner, use 1/3 cup toasted pepitas and check packaged ingredients for allergen cross-contact.
Delicata squash is not a direct size-for-size swap: use three medium squash, make six portions and begin checking for tenderness after 25 minutes.
storage: Cool leftovers within 2 hours and refrigerate the stuffed squash in a shallow airtight container for up to 4 days. Reheat covered in a 375°F oven for 15 to 20 minutes, uncover for 5 minutes to restore the top, and verify the center reaches 165°F. The cooked filling can be frozen for up to 2 months; freeze it separately when possible because thawed squash flesh becomes softer. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator before reheating.
notes: Acorn squash vary in density. Use the knife-tender test rather than color alone, and start checking smaller halves at 35 minutes so their shells remain sturdy enough to fill.
Wheat berries are sold as hard, soft, spring or winter wheat. Any whole variety works here, but older or especially hard berries may need up to 10 extra minutes and more water.

If preparing ahead, cook the filling and roast the squash up to 2 days in advance. Refrigerate them separately, fill the cold halves and allow 18 to 22 minutes for the final 425°F bake to reach 165°F.
To serve this as a holiday side rather than a meatless main, cut each roasted half crosswise after reheating to make eight smaller portions; use a sharp knife so the skins do not collapse.
Calories and cost estimate one filled squash half per serving and will vary with squash size, oil absorption, walnut prices and local produce costs.

faqs.q: Do wheat berries need to be soaked before cooking?
faqs.a: No. Unsoaked wheat berries become chewy-tender in roughly 45 to 55 minutes here. An overnight soak can shorten that time, but drain the berries, begin checking at 30 minutes and still cook until the hard white center disappears.

faqs.q: Can I eat the skin of roasted acorn squash?
faqs.a: Yes, the scrubbed skin is edible after thorough roasting, though its firmness varies by squash and preference. The sturdy shell is useful as a bowl; diners can scoop the soft flesh away from it if they do not enjoy the skin.

faqs.q: Why is my stuffed acorn squash watery?
faqs.a: The mushrooms, grains or lentils likely retained excess moisture. Brown mushrooms until their liquid evaporates, drain the cooked wheat berries and canned lentils thoroughly, and make sure no liquid pools in the skillet before filling the roasted halves.
